inline: "Top web developer" is a marketing phrase, not a credential. There is no industry certification, no authoritative ranking, and no single agency that is objectively "the best" for every project. Search for "top web developers offering ecommerce websites" and you will find listicles that are almost entirely pay-to-play: directories where placement is bought, not earned.

items: Years in business.
Number of projects delivered.

Awards, directory placements, or "top agency" badges.
Aggregate review scores.

blocks.text: What "top" should actually mean for your project

items: Depth on the specific platform you are using, not general web experience.
Stores you can open, test on mobile, and check out on — not screenshots.
Load time, conversion, or order volume changes they can cite.
Staging, QA, milestones, and change-order handling that are documented.
A clear maintenance and warranty arrangement, not a disappearing act after go-live.

inline: If a developer cannot speak to all five, their "top" claim is not relevant to your project, no matter how many badges they display. This is the same principle the vetting section of our
is built around.
These five criteria are what actually differentiate a top ecommerce developer from a merely popular one. Run every candidate through them in the same order.

The developer should specialise in the platform your store runs on, not offer "ecommerce on any platform." A brilliant Shopify developer will struggle on a headless Next.js build, and vice versa. Ask for the platform they have built the most stores on, and verify it against their portfolio. For platform-specific vetting, see

inline: Ask for three live ecommerce stores. Then open each one on mobile and go through the checkout yourself. This is the single most reliable signal in the entire evaluation, and it takes ten minutes. A developer with a genuinely strong portfolio will encourage this; a developer with a weak one will send screenshots instead.

A top developer cites numbers: load time before and after, conversion rate lift, order volume change, or post-launch bug count. A weak developer cites only aesthetics. The specific metrics matter less than the habit of measuring — the developers who track results are also the ones who understand why their work matters.

Ask how they handle staging, QA, milestones, change requests, and handover. A top developer has a documented process and will describe it without prompting. A weak developer will say "we figure it out as we go." This is where most mid-market projects fail, and it is entirely avoidable.

Ask what happens after launch: warranty period, maintenance options, response times, and what is in scope for the retainer. A top developer has a clear answer and a written agreement. A weak developer goes quiet after the final invoice, which is when most of the real work (maintenance, bug fixes, iteration) begins.

sections.title: Comparison Framework: How to Score Finalists

inline: Use the table below to compare three to five finalists on the same criteria. Score each candidate 1 to 5 on each row, then total. This forces a structured comparison instead of a gut decision driven by the last sales call.

head: Criterion
What to look for
Score (1-5)
rows: Specialises in your platform, has built multiple stores on it
Three live URLs that pass a mobile checkout test
Cites specific numbers (load time, conversion, order volume)
Documented staging, QA, milestones, change orders, handover
Written warranty, maintenance options, defined response times
Two recent references willing to speak by phone
Written scope, payment milestones, IP ownership, change-order terms

inline: Add the totals. If two finalists are within 2 points of each other, weight platform fit and reference quality highest — those are the criteria that predict actual project success. If a candidate scores below 3 on any single row, do not hire them regardless of their total score, because a single weak criterion (process, support, or references) usually turns out to be the failure point of the project.

blocks.text: What a strong score looks like

inline: A top developer typically scores 4 or 5 on all seven rows, with the reference quality row scoring highest. That pattern — where the developer's own clients are the strongest evidence — is the clearest signal of a genuinely top-tier developer.

blocks.text: What a weak score looks like

inline: A well-marketed developer with a weak actual portfolio often scores high on the "years in business" and "client logos" they present voluntarily, but low on the criteria above once you probe. This is why the criteria matter: marketing material and actual capability diverge sharply in this market.

sections.title: Vetting Questions That Separate the Top from the Rest

inline: These questions are not the same as the general 12-question vetting list in the pillar guide. They are specifically designed to test the difference between a well-marketed developer and a genuinely top one. Ask them in this order.

b: "Which platform do you specialise in, and why that one?"

items: A top developer gives a specific, confident answer and can name trade-offs. A weak developer claims to do everything.

b: "Show me three live stores you built, and tell me what you did on each."

items: A top developer opens their laptop and walks you through the stores. A weak developer sends a PDF or a link to a theme demo.

b: "What was the measured result on your most successful project?"

items: A top developer cites specific numbers. A weak developer cites "high client satisfaction" or avoids the question.

b: "Walk me through how you handle a mid-project change request."

items: A top developer describes a written change-order process with a clear cost and timeline impact. A weak developer says "we'll figure it out."

b: "Who specifically will work on my project, and what is their platform experience?"

items: A top developer names the team. A weak developer hides behind "our team" or "our global capability."

b: "What happens after launch — warranty, maintenance, response times?"

items: A top developer has a written answer. A weak developer treats this as a future problem.

b: "Can I speak to two recent clients whose projects are similar to mine?"

items: A top developer readily provides references. A weak developer stalls, or provides references that cannot speak to the work.

b: "What could go wrong on my project, and how would you handle it?"

items: A top developer names specific risks and specific mitigations. A weak developer says "we don't expect any issues," which is the single biggest red flag in the entire call.

sections.title: Red Flags in a "Top Developer" Claim

inline: The developers with the strongest marketing are not always the strongest developers. These are the signals that a "top" claim is marketing, not capability.

items: Portfolio shows screenshots, not live URLs.
Portfolio stores are stock theme demos with brand colours swapped.
Portfolio mixes content sites and ecommerce stores with no distinction — suggests ecommerce is a side offering, not a specialism.
Claims deep expertise in every platform (Shopify, WooCommerce, Magento, headless, custom) — no one is genuinely deep on all of them.
Cites award badges prominently without specifics on the projects that earned them.
Uses "we" heavily without naming who will work on your project.
Cannot provide two recent references.
Requests full payment upfront, or refuses to define milestones.
Has no documented QA or staging process.
Treats the contract as a formality to sign after the project starts.

If you have three to five finalists who all score well on the framework above, the decision usually comes down to four tiebreakers.

The developer whose references are the most willing to speak openly is usually the safest bet. A reference who says "honestly, here's what went wrong and how they handled it" is worth more than three references who give generic praise.
A developer who has built five stores exactly like yours is a better choice than one who has built twenty different kinds. Specificity of experience predicts success more reliably than breadth.

The developer who showed you the most of their process — staging, milestones, QA, change orders — is usually the one who will communicate best during the project. Process transparency during the sales process predicts process transparency during delivery.

You will spend weeks or months working with this developer. If the calls are uncomfortable, the written updates are vague, or the communication style does not match yours, the project will be harder even if the technical work is strong.

blocks.text: What should not be a tiebreaker

items: A 20 percent price difference is small compared to the cost of a failed build. If a developer is dramatically cheaper than the others, that is worth examining, not celebrating.
They are marketing, not evidence.
A developer who built one small page for a famous brand is not necessarily better than one who built ten full stores for mid-market clients.

faqs.q: How do I find the top web developers offering ecommerce websites?
a: Start with referrals from store owners you trust, then verify each candidate against the five criteria above: platform fit, live portfolio, measurable results, process maturity, and post-launch support. Avoid directory listicles, which are usually pay-to-play.

Usually not. Most are pay-to-play: agencies pay for placement, and rankings reflect marketing spend rather than capability. The exception is platform-specific partner directories (e.g., Shopify Partners), which are a weaker signal but not entirely paid.

faqs.q: Should I hire the cheapest top developer?
a: No. A 20 percent price difference is small compared to the cost of a failed build. Compare on the five criteria first, then use price as a tiebreaker only between finalists who all score well.

faqs.q: How many developers should I shortlist?
a: Three to five is the right range. Fewer than three and you have no real comparison; more than five and you will confuse yourself. The point of a shortlist is to compare, not to exhaust the market.

faqs.q: What is the single most reliable vetting signal?
a: Live portfolio stores you can open on mobile and take through checkout yourself. A developer with three live, functional ecommerce stores is almost always a legitimate ecommerce developer. A developer with no live stores is not.

faqs.q: Do top developers always cost more?
a: Usually, but not always. The premium reflects delivery reliability and process maturity more than pure skill. For a small, well-scoped project, a mid-tier developer can deliver excellent work at a lower price. For a complex or high-stakes build, the premium is usually worth it. See

faqs.q: How do I verify a developer's claimed results?
a: Ask for two client references and for live URLs of the stores in question. Open the stores yourself, and ask the references specifically what changed. Claims without verification are marketing, not evidence.

inline: Shortlist three to five candidates, score them on the framework above, and use reference quality and scope fit as your tiebreakers. A structured comparison is the single most reliable way to avoid a bad hire in this market.
